title: What Sunday Family Dinners Taught Me About Belonging
script: Narrator: [warmly] Every Sunday, without exception, my whole family gathers at my aunt's house for dinner. It has been this way since I was a child.
Narrator: [thoughtful] As a teenager, I found these dinners boring. I wanted to be anywhere else, with my own friends instead.
Narrator: [honestly] I used to sit quietly, checking the time, waiting for a polite moment to leave early.
Narrator: [reflective] Then I moved to another city for work, and Sunday dinners suddenly stopped happening for me completely.
Narrator: [softly] At first, I enjoyed the freedom. No more long dinners, no more loud cousins arguing about small things.
Narrator: [honestly] But after a few months, something felt missing, even though my new life was busy and full.
Narrator: [thoughtful] I started calling my mother more, just to hear updates about who said what at dinner that week.
Narrator: [warmly] Slowly, I realized those dinners were never really about the food. They were about simply being counted, being present.
Narrator: [reflective] My grandmother once said a family that eats together rarely feels truly alone, even during hard years.
Narrator: [gently] I understand her words differently now, from far away, than I ever did sitting at that crowded table.
Narrator: [determined] So now, whenever I visit home, I make Sunday dinner my absolute priority, no matter what else is planned.
Narrator: [warmly] My cousins still argue loudly about small things, and somehow, now, I find that noise comforting instead of annoying.
Narrator: [peacefully] Belonging, I learned, is not always exciting. Sometimes it is just showing up, again and again, for ordinary Sundays.
Narrator: [with feeling] I hope my own future children will complain about these dinners too, and later miss them just as much as I did.
